procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused, being aggrieved by the High Court's judgment and sentence, filed Special Leave Petitions (SLPs) before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court granted leave to appeal in the SLPs, converting them into Criminal Appeals. In one case (SLP (Crl.) No. 5296 of 2012), leave was granted during the proceedings. On 11.05.2009, the Supreme Court noted that the appellants had served seven years in prison and could be granted bail on the satisfaction of the Trial Court of necessary conditions. The appeals were partly allowed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the misjoinder of charges caused prejudice to the appellant and could be considered fatal to the prosecution's case.

facts: The appellant was convicted for an offence under Section 364A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
However, the charge framed by the Sessions Judge did not include all the necessary ingredients of the offence under Section 364A.
Specifically, the charge failed to state that the kidnapping was for ransom, which is a key element of that particular offence.
law: The court must frame a charge that accurately describes the offence alleged against the accused.
An accused should not suffer any prejudice due to a misjoinder or improper framing of charges.
While courts have the power to alter or add charges under Section 216 of the Cr.PC, this power is constrained by the prejudice likely to be caused to the accused.
If the ingredients of a higher offence are not put to the accused while framing the charge, it can cause prejudice.
application: The Supreme Court found that it was obligatory for the trial court to frame a charge that included all the elements of Section 364A, including the motive of ransom.
By failing to do so, the trial court did not properly inform the appellant of the full accusation against him.
This omission was not a minor error but a failure to put the ingredients of a "higher offence" to the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the failure to properly frame the charge caused "apparent prejudice" to the appellant. Because the specific ingredients of the offence under Section 364A were not put to him, his conviction under that section was ruled unsustainable. Therefore, the misjoinder was considered fatal to the prosecution's case for the conviction under Section 364A.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the misjoinder of charges caused prejudice to the appellant and could be considered fatal to the prosecution's case.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's counsel placed reliance on the precedent set in Sk. Ahmed vs. State of Telangana, (2021) 9 SCC 59, implying that the principles from that case regarding misjoinder of charges should be applied.
respondent_arguments: The respondent-State supported the judgment of the High Court.
The respondent contended that there is no merit in the appeals and they should be dismissed.
The respondent submitted that the High Court was justified in its reasoning and in dismissing the appeals.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a legal provision requires the fulfillment of multiple conditions connected by the word 'and', all conditions must be established.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court, relying on precedents such as Sk. Ahmed v. State of Telangana, found that a misjoinder of charges is impermissible if it causes prejudice to the appellant or results in a failure of justice. Applying this principle, the court determined that the conviction under Section 364A of the IPC could not be sustained.
legal_tests_applied: The propositions of law which can be culled out from the aforementioned judgments are:(i) The appellant should not suffer any prejudice by reason of misjoinder of charges. (iii) It should not result in failure of justice.
policy_considerations: The appellant should not suffer any prejudice by reason of misjoinder of charges.
A misjoinder of charges should not result in failure of justice.
